Tower
TOU-'r
n. (rendering Hebrew migdāl and Greek purgos)
From Old French tur, from Latin turris, a high structure. The Hebrew migdāl comes from gādal, to be great, to grow, to magnify — a tower is literally a greatening, a made-tall thing. That etymology is the whole moral history of the tower in Scripture, because the same root that builds a refuge builds a boast, and the difference between the two is whose name is on it.

Biblical Definition

Scripture sets two towers against each other and the contrast is exact. At Babel men said, “Go to, let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name” (Gen 11:4) — a tower built upward out of fear of being scattered, and built expressly to secure a name for the builders. The LORD came down to see the city and the tower which the children of men builded, and the making of a name ended in the confusion of speech. Over against it stands Solomon's proverb: “The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe” (Pro 18:10). The one tower is climbed to make a name; the other is a name, and it is entered by running rather than built by labour. Between these lie the ordinary towers of the working world — the watchtower in the vineyard, built to guard fruit (Isa 5:2), and the tower of the parable whose builder must sit down first and count the cost, lest all that behold begin to mock him (Luk 14:28). That parable is the Lord's own warning against undertaking discipleship as a project of enthusiasm, and it stands directly beside the Babel account in sense: the man who builds without reckoning and the men who build to make a name both end mocked, and both end scattered from what they meant to raise.

Webster 1828 Definition

A high structure raised for defence, watching, or display; in Scripture divided between the tower of Babel, built upward to make a name and ending in confusion, and the name of the LORD, which is a strong tower entered by the righteous who run into it.

TOWER, n. 1. A building, either round or square, raised to a considerable elevation, and consisting of several stories.

2. A fortress; a citadel; a place of defense or of watching. Thou hast been a shelter for me, and a strong tower from the enemy. Psalm 61.

3. In Scripture, a figure of the divine protection. The name of the LORD is a strong tower. Prov. 18.

4. A watchtower in a vineyard or field, built for the keeper who guarded the fruit in the season. Isa. 5; Matt. 21.

5. The tower of Babel; the structure built in the plain of Shinar, whose top was to reach to heaven, and at which the language of the builders was confounded. Gen. 11.

Key Scripture

Genesis 11:4 — "And they said, Go to, let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name, lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth."

Proverbs 18:10 — "The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe."

Luke 14:28 — "For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?"

Nehemiah 2:17 — "Then said I unto them, Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste, and the gates thereof are burned with fire: come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach."

Modern Corruption

Babel is retold as a myth explaining language diversity, or admired as a symbol of human aspiration wrongly punished by a jealous God, when the text presents it as an act of self-naming judged in mercy.

expand to see more

The common academic handling treats Gen 11 as an aetiological legend composed to explain why nations speak differently — a story about language rather than an event with a judgment in it. This assumes what it should prove, namely that the early chapters of Genesis are not historical narrative. Moses writes them as history, with a place (a plain in the land of Shinar), a technology (brick for stone, and slime for morter), a stated motive (let us make us a name), and a consequence. The genealogy of Gen 10 already presumes the dispersion, and Gen 11 supplies its cause. The text is not accounting for a curiosity; it is recording a rebellion and its remedy.

The second and more flattering misreading admires the builders. Babel becomes the emblem of human aspiration, ambition, and unity, checked by a God who resents His creatures' reach. But Scripture nowhere condemns building, height, or skill; Bezaleel was filled with the Spirit of God for craftsmanship, and the temple was magnificent. What is condemned at Babel is the purpose — let us make us a name — which is the exact inversion of the promise God would shortly make to Abram: I will make thy name great. One name is seized and one is given. And the scattering was mercy, not spite: a united humanity in that condition would have been a greater tyranny, and the confusion of tongues that judged Babel was answered at Pentecost, when men of every nation heard the wonderful works of God each in his own language.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew migdāl, from gādal (to be great), names the tower as a made-great thing; it appears in place-names such as Migdal-el and in the tower of the flock, Migdal-eder. Greek purgos covers watchtower, fortress, and the tower of the parables.

expand to see more

Hebrew migdāl (H4026) — a tower, a raised platform; from gādal (H1431), to grow great, to magnify — the same root behind gedullah, greatness.

Hebrew 'ōphel (H6076) — a mound or stronghold, rendered tower in Isa 32:14 and used of the fortified rise in Jerusalem south of the temple.

Hebrew bābel (H894) — Babel, Babylon; the Babylonians derived it as the gate of god, but Moses ties it by sound to bālal (H1101), to confound.

Greek purgos (G4444) — a tower; used of the tower in the vineyard (Mat 21:33), the tower of Siloam that fell (Luk 13:4), and the tower of the counting-the-cost parable.

Greek onoma (G3686) — name; the word that carries the whole contrast, since Babel sought a name for itself and Pro 18:10 makes the name of the LORD the refuge.

Usage

"Of defence and refuge: a strong tower from the enemy (Psa 61:3); the name of the LORD is a strong tower (Pro 18:10)."

"Of watching over fruit and flock: he built a tower in the midst of it (Isa 5:2); the tower of the flock, Migdal-eder (Mic 4:8)."

"Of presumption and its judgment: a tower whose top may reach unto heaven (Gen 11:4); a builder who did not count the cost (Luk 14:28)."
